paragraphs.heading: What entropy measures
paragraphs.text: Entropy is a property of a system's state that describes how its possible microstates are spread out. A microstate is one particular arrangement of the system's atoms and molecules. Ludwig Boltzmann explained entropy as a measure of how many such arrangements fit the large-scale condition we observe. The idea began in classical thermodynamics and now reaches into statistical physics and information theory. It is used in chemistry, biology, cosmology, economics and telecommunication.

paragraphs.heading: The second law
paragraphs.text: Entropy sits at the heart of the second law of thermodynamics. That law says an isolated system left to change on its own can never lose entropy as time passes. So such systems drift toward equilibrium, where entropy is highest. High entropy means energy is spread evenly through a system, while low entropy means it is bunched in one or a few spots. One result is that some processes cannot be undone.

paragraphs.heading: Falling heat
paragraphs.text: Early hints came from machines. In 1803 Lazare Carnot argued that in any machine the jolts of moving parts waste activity, and that natural processes tend to dissipate useful energy. His son Sadi Carnot wrote in 1824 that heat engines make work as heat falls from a hot body to a cold one, much as water falls through a water wheel. That was an early insight into the second law.

paragraphs.heading: Clausius names it
paragraphs.text: The first law, which is about energy being conserved, could not separately measure the effects of friction and waste. In the 1850s and 1860s Rudolf Clausius looked closely at the usable heat lost when work is done, such as heat made by friction. He found that unusable energy grows as steam moves from inlet to exhaust in a steam engine. In 1865 he defined the quantity as a tiny amount of heat divided by the temperature at that moment, and named it entropy, from a Greek word meaning turning or change. English took up the word in 1868.

paragraphs.heading: A word like energy
paragraphs.text: Clausius built the new word by swapping the root of the Greek ergon, meaning work, for that of tropē, meaning transformation. He shaped it on purpose to sound like energy, because he found the two quantities nearly analogous in their physical meaning. Leon Cooper later remarked that Clausius had made a word meaning the same thing to everyone: nothing.

paragraphs.heading: Counting arrangements
paragraphs.text: Later, Boltzmann, Josiah Willard Gibbs and James Clerk Maxwell put entropy on a statistical footing. In 1877 Boltzmann found a way to measure the entropy of an ideal gas using probability. In his definition, entropy rises in proportion to the natural logarithm of how many microstates the gas could occupy. The constant in that rule, the Boltzmann constant, is now one of the defining constants of the International System of Units, or SI.

paragraphs.heading: Two views, one idea
paragraphs.text: There are two main ways to describe entropy. The classical view uses quantities you can measure in bulk, such as mass, volume, pressure and temperature. The statistical view uses the motions of a system's tiny parts, first treated as Newtonian particles of a gas and later in quantum terms. Together they give one consistent picture of the second law, which applies to physical processes everywhere.
